title: Sweeping Out the Old Yeast
sum: Paul turns from the quarrels of chapters 1-4 to a case he has heard about: a man in the church is living with his father's wife. Paul is shocked, not by the man so much as by the church's pride in being open-minded about it. He tells them to gather, in the name of the Lord Jesus, and put the man out, "for the ruin of his flesh, so that on the day of the Lord his spirit may be saved."

He then explains the rule with a picture from Passover: a little yeast spreads through the whole dough, and our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered, so the church must be unleavened bread. In 5:9-13 he corrects a misunderstanding of his earlier letter. He never meant them to avoid every sinner in the world, only to refuse table fellowship to a person who bears the name of brother and lives in open sin. God judges outsiders; the church must deal with its own.
readings: Read as church discipline

The chapter is the New Testament's main example of excluding a member for sin. Its words, "hand over to Satan" and "do not even eat," are the base for every later practice of excommunication, the ban and shunning, and each tradition has read them in the light of Matthew 18:15-18 (see the card).
Read as a Passover sermon
5:6-8 is built on the feast of Unleavened Bread. Christ's death is the Passover lamb's, so the church is fresh dough. The discipline is not cruelty but cleaning the house for the feast.
Read as a lesson in status and pride

The Corinthians were "puffed up," not grieving. A rich or well-connected man could protect an offender, and the church may have counted tolerance as a mark of freedom. Paul reverses their view of what is shameful.

views.H: The woman is called his father's wife, not his mother (5:1). Roman law forbade marrying a stepmother (Gaius, Institutes 1.63), and Paul says the Gentiles do not do it. The man probably had standing: some scholars propose that he was a patron whose influence kept the church quiet. The earlier letter (5:9) is lost. Paul is writing from Ephesus; 16:8 has him planning to stay until Pentecost, which may place the letter in the spring, and the Passover picture may or may not mean he wrote near the feast.
views.C: The grammar of 5:3-5 is disputed: the phrase "in the name of our Lord Jesus" can be joined to "I have judged" or to "when you are gathered." Textual variants add "Christ" in 5:4 and "Jesus" in 5:5, and the KJV adds "named" in 5:1 (see the variants). Some scholars see 2 Corinthians 2:5-11 and 7:12 as a later look at this same case; others think they refer to a different offender. The proposal that 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1 came from the lost letter of 5:9 is one view among several.
views.L: Chapters 5-6 are a unit of three scandals (the stepmother, the lawsuit, the prostitute), each handled by "Do you not know" questions and an appeal to the church's identity. In this chapter the picture of yeast and dough links the case (5:1-5) to the Passover (5:6-8) and then to the clarification (5:9-13). The refrain from Deuteronomy at the end, "Remove the evil person," closes the chapter and echoes the "taken out from among you" of 5:2.
views.J: The offense is named in the Torah (Leviticus 18:8; Leviticus 20:11; Deuteronomy 22:30; Deuteronomy 27:20). Leviticus 20:11 sets the penalty of death, while Deuteronomy 27:20 is a curse and 22:30 a prohibition. Paul changes the penalty to removal and borrows Deuteronomy's refrain for capital crimes (for example 17:7). He reads Passover for Gentiles who never lived in Egypt. A Jewish reader sees a Jew using Torah to hold a mostly Gentile church to a Jewish standard, and also sees Christ placed where the lamb of Exodus 12 stood. The Mishnah (Sanhedrin 7:4) later lists relations with a father's wife among the offenses punished by stoning.
views.T: The "handing over to Satan" has been read as expulsion (Chrysostom stresses the aim of repentance), as bodily affliction (some of the Fathers and many modern readers), and as an act of the whole church (Calvin). The verse is the base of the Catholic power of excommunication, the Lutheran ban, the Reformed censures and the Anabaptist shunning. The Roman rite offers 5:6-8 as an optional second reading on Easter Sunday: our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered, therefore keep the feast.

deep.b:
Paul says only that "a man has his father's wife." The words suggest a stepmother, not the man's own mother, and that the union was still going on. Whether the father was alive, dead or divorced is not stated. Roman law barred marriage to a stepmother, and the Torah bars the union as an offense against the father (Leviticus 18:8). Paul says it is a kind not found even among the Gentiles.

Two further points matter. First, Paul blames the church more than the man: he does not tell them to judge the man's guilt, because he has already judged (5:3), but to act. Second, nothing is said about the woman, who is perhaps not a believer, since Paul says in 5:12 that he does not judge outsiders. Reading the chapter as a general law about adultery would miss how specific it is.

On the eve of the fourteenth of Nisan, Jewish households search the house for leaven and remove it, because Exodus 12:15 says leaven must be cleared out. Paul says the church is already "unleavened," meaning cleansed in Christ, and must therefore act like it: "Sweep out the old yeast." The picture runs in two directions. The yeast stands for the malice and evil of sin that can spread; the unleavened bread stands for sincerity and truth. The Christian festival is not one week but all of life. The Roman rite's Easter Sunday reading takes up exactly this line.

Paul does not say the church should keep Passover on a calendar, and whether it did is not known. (16:8 shows only that he dates his plans by Pentecost.) What matters for the Corinthians is that the death of Christ is the reason for holiness, not just its reward.

deep.h: Inside and outside: the limit of the rule
deep.b: The Corinthians had misread the earlier letter as a call to withdraw from all sinners. Paul replies that they would have to leave the world. His rule has two edges: it applies only to a person who is named a brother or sister, and it is about closeness (eating, 5:11), not about doing business or living in the same town. God judges outsiders (5:13). The list in 5:11 puts sexual sin beside greed, idol worship, slander, drunkenness and swindling, so the rule is not a ban on one kind of sin. In the same way, it is set against the church's own habit of excusing a famous member.

echoes: Leviticus 18:8; Leviticus 20:11; Deuteronomy 22:30; Deuteronomy 27:20; Deuteronomy 17:7; Exodus 12:15; Matthew 18:15; 2 Corinthians 2:5; 2 Corinthians 7:12; 1 Timothy 1:20; Galatians 5:9

settings.what: Paul's verdict on the man and his father's wife
settings.to: The whole church at Corinth, gathered as an assembly, not the man or a council of leaders
settings.when: After Paul heard a report (the text says only that it is 'reported'; Chloe's people in 1:11 or Stephanas' visit in 16:17 are possible sources), perhaps in the spring, since 16:8 has Paul in Ephesus until Pentecost (the season is not certain)
settings.why: To make a proud church act, and to show that tolerance of this case is not freedom but a danger to the whole body. The Passover picture tells them why: they have been cleansed and must live as cleansed people. Paul's aim for the man is rescue, 'that his spirit may be saved.'
settings.readers: A mostly Gentile church in a Roman colony that prized honor, patronage and freedom. Some may have admired the man's boldness or were afraid to offend a patron.
views: The purpose is to keep the sin from spreading, like yeast (5:6).
The purpose is his repentance and final salvation (5:5), the view of Chrysostom and many modern readers.
Most commentators hold that both aims are in the text.

settings.what: Paul's correction of his earlier letter
settings.to: The church at Corinth, who had taken his earlier advice 'not to mix with sexual sinners' too widely
settings.when: As he answers the news from Corinth and before he turns to the church's own letter at 7:1
settings.why: To say exactly whom the rule covers: a believer who lives in open, unrepentant sin, not all unbelievers. Outsiders are God's to judge; the church deals with its own.
settings.readers: Believers whose daily lives were full of non-Christian neighbors and business partners, to whom they could not simply refuse contact.

traditions.q: How should a church treat a member who lives in open, unrepentant sin?
views: Excommunication, the Church's gravest penalty, is a medicinal penalty (Code of Canon Law, canons 1312 and 1331) that bars a person from the sacraments (Catechism 1463; canon 1331). Only the Pope, the local bishop or priests they authorize can lift it, though any priest can absolve a person in danger of death (Catechism 1463).

Exclusion from Holy Communion can be a penance (epitimia) given by a spiritual father or priest as medicine for the soul; the penitent may not commune until the confessor grants absolution and blesses it.

The Augsburg Confession (article 28) says bishops may "exclude from the communion of the Church wicked men, whose wickedness is known," by the Word alone and without force. The Smalcald Articles (III.9, "Of Excommunication") say manifest and obstinate sinners are not admitted to the Sacrament until they amend, and that no civil penalties are to be joined to this discipline.

Discipline is a mark of a true church (Belgic Confession, article 29). The Westminster Confession (chapter 30) names three steps: admonition, suspension from the Lord's Supper for a season, and excommunication, carried out by church officers.

Schleitheim (article 2) sets the ban for baptized members who fall into error and sin: two private admonitions, and the third time open discipline or the ban. The Dordrecht Confession (article 17) says the separated person is to be shunned by the other members, including in eating and drinking (compare 5:11).

The local congregation as a whole holds the authority. The 1689 Confession (chapter 26) says Christ gave each gathered church "all that power and authority, which is in any way needful for their carrying on that order in worship and discipline," and that members are under "the censures and government thereof."

title: Courts, Vices and the Body
sum: Paul's second case is a lawsuit. One believer has taken another to a pagan court. He is astonished: the saints will judge the world and angels, so can they not settle a dispute over property? It would be better to be wronged. Then he warns that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God, lists the kinds of people he means, and says, "And some of you were like this. But you were washed. But you were made holy. But you were justified."

The rest of the chapter answers two slogans from Corinth, "Everything is permitted for me" and "Foods are for the stomach." Paul agrees that all is allowed in principle, but not everything helps, and he will not be mastered by anything. The body is not like the stomach: it is for the Lord and will be raised. To join it to a prostitute makes one body with her. So "run away from sexual sin" and "bring glory to God with your body."
readings: Read as an argument from status
Corinth was a city of lawsuits and honor. The case is about wealthy members using the courts against poorer ones, and the church's reputation among outsiders.
Read as a lesson on the body
6:12-20 is the New Testament's main passage on the body as the Spirit's temple and on the bond made by sex. It is read in the light of resurrection (6:14) and the Eucharist.
Read as a debate with slogans

Much of 6:12-20 sounds like Paul answering things the Corinthians said to him: "Everything is permitted," "Foods are for the stomach." Whether or not each line is a quotation, the argument works by Paul granting a point and then drawing a line.

views.H: Roman courts favored the rich, and a lawsuit between members of different standing would have been a public matter. Corinth was a colony of freed slaves and veterans, proud of its commerce, and known for its sexual license. Banquets could end with prostitutes. Paul writes of what the weight of the body means in a place where sex was taken as a bodily appetite on a par with eating.
views.C: Textual points are few: the KJV adds "and in your spirit, which are God's" in 6:20, and the NA28 adds "Christ" in 6:11 (see the variants). The main critical debate is about the slogans (6:12, 13, 18) and about malakoi and arsenokoitai in 6:9, one of them, arsenokoitai, being a word not found in any certain earlier text (see the notes).
views.L: The chapter uses "Do you not know" six times (6:2, 3, 9, 15, 16, 19), each time to call the Corinthians back to what they were taught. The sections are balanced: a case (6:1-8), a list and the great reversal (6:9-11), and a second argument (6:12-20) that runs from permission to purchase. The three verbs of 6:11, "washed ... made holy ... justified," are in the past tense, against the present list of vices.
views.J: Jews were allowed to judge their own members under Roman rule, and the later rabbis taught against going to Gentile courts (Talmud, Gittin 88b). Paul's quotation of Genesis 2:24 in 6:16 shows how he reads the Torah on the bond of sex. The list of vices in 6:9-10 resembles Jewish lists, and the pair arsenokoitai plausibly draws on the Greek of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13. "Temple" language (6:19) is Jewish language applied to the body.
views.T: The "soft men" and the "men who lie with males" are the center of the modern church debate on same-sex relations (see the card). Chrysostom and other Fathers preached on 6:12-20 against sexual sin of every kind, and the picture of the body as the Spirit's temple became a standard theme of Christian teaching on chastity.

deep.h: Why go to court? Lawsuits and honor
deep.b:
In a Roman colony, the courts were the field of honor. A person sued to win a public contest as much as to win money, and being sued was a shame. Some scholars think the Corinthian cases were brought by the church's more powerful members, in the style of the city's elites. Paul's answer works at three levels. First, the saints will judge the world. Second, a church that cannot settle small cases looks foolish to outsiders. Third, taking the loss is better than winning a case in an unbeliever's court, because the real defeat is the quarrel itself.

The passage does not say that believers may never go to a court; it deals with a case between members of the church. The later church built its own courts partly on this passage.

deep.h: "And some of you were like this"
deep.b:
The list in 6:9-10 has ten kinds of people, and 6:11 tells the Corinthians that some of them were once such people. Three things have changed them: they were washed, made holy and justified. The same event is described three ways. Paul says nothing in this passage about how often the sins were committed or whether any of them was a one-time act. The point is the change of identity: a new name has replaced the old one.

Of the ten, the sexual terms are the best known today. The words malakoi and arsenokoitai are discussed in the notes at 6:9. They have no certain English equivalent, and the Plain translates them literally and lets the reader weigh the debate.

deep.h: The body, the stomach and the bond of sex
deep.b:
The Corinthian argument seems to have run: food and the stomach go together, and God will bring both to an end, so sex and the body go together in the same way and do not matter. Paul answers that the body is different. It is for the Lord, it has been bought, it will be raised (6:14), and it belongs to Christ (6:15). Joined to a prostitute, it becomes one body with her. Joined to the Lord, it becomes one spirit with him. The Spirit lives in it as in a temple.

The passage is also one of Paul's clearest statements that the body is not unimportant. It is a rebuke to the view that the soul alone matters, and to the view that what is done with the body is private.

echoes: Genesis 2:24; Daniel 7:22; Leviticus 18:22; Leviticus 20:13; Matthew 5:39; Matthew 19:5; Romans 1:26; Romans 6:15; Romans 8:11; 1 Timothy 1:10; Acts 22:16; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 1:18

settings.what: Paul's rebuke over lawsuits between believers
settings.to: The church at Corinth, especially members with property disputes
settings.when: As he answers reports of how the church is behaving, between the case of 5:1 and the church's letter at 7:1
settings.why: To shame the church out of taking its quarrels to unbelievers, and to remind members that they will judge the world. The warning of 6:9-11 reminds them what kind of kingdom they belong to, and what they were.
settings.readers: Believers in a city of lawsuits and rivalry, some wealthy, many poor, who had imported the habit of public contests for honor into the church.
views: Some scholars read the suits as brought by wealthier members.
Others stress that the text covers any quarrel, not just class conflicts.

settings.what: Paul's answer to the slogans about freedom and the body
settings.to: The Corinthians, especially those who claimed that bodily acts are morally neutral, and men who used prostitutes
settings.when: As he moves from the vice list to sexual sin, which was the sin the earlier letter had addressed (5:9)
settings.why: To show that freedom is limited by what helps and by what masters us, and that the body belongs to the Lord, has been bought and will be raised. Sex is not like eating.
settings.readers: A church in a port city where men's sexual freedom was assumed, and where some taught that the body did not matter because only the spirit was saved.

traditions.q: What do the words translated 'soft men' and 'men who lie with males' name, and what does each church teach about same-sex relations?
views: The pair is read as covering same-sex acts. The Catechism lists 1 Corinthians 6:10 among the texts that present same-sex acts as grave sin and teaches that such acts are "intrinsically disordered" (§2357); persons with same-sex attraction are to be treated with respect and called to chastity (§2358-2359).
The pair is read as covering same-sex acts. Chrysostom, in his homily on Romans 1:26-27, calls such acts contrary to nature (Homily 4 on Romans).

The Southern Baptist Convention's Baptist Faith and Message 2000 defines marriage as "the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime" (article XVIII) and lists homosexuality among the sexual immoralities Christians should oppose (article XV).

Divided. The Westminster Larger Catechism (question 139) lists sodomy and "all unnatural lusts" among the sins the seventh commandment forbids. The Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) changed the Book of Order's definition of marriage in 2014-2015 (Amendment 14-F, "a unique relationship between two people, traditionally a man and a woman"). On the words of 6:9 themselves, writers argue both ways. Robert Gagnon reads the pair as naming same-sex intercourse itself, with malakoi as males who take the female role. Dale Martin argues that arsenokoitai pointed to some kind of economic exploitation by means of sex, not necessarily homosexual sex, and that malakos is better rendered "effeminate"; he adds that he does not claim to know what arsenokoites meant, only that no one does. The notes on 6:9 set out the evidence.

Divided. The Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod has said, in a 1973 resolution restated by its president in 2009, that homosexual behavior is "intrinsically sinful"; the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America voted in 2009 to open its ministry to partnered gay and lesbian pastors. On the words of 6:9 themselves, writers argue both ways. Robert Gagnon reads the pair as naming same-sex intercourse itself, with malakoi as males who take the female role. Dale Martin argues that arsenokoitai pointed to some kind of economic exploitation by means of sex, not necessarily homosexual sex, and that malakos is better rendered "effeminate"; he adds that he does not claim to know what arsenokoites meant, only that no one does. The notes on 6:9 set out the evidence.

Divided. The Lambeth Conference of 1998 (resolution I.10) rejected "homosexual practice as incompatible with Scripture" and said the bishops "cannot advise the legitimising or blessing of same sex unions"; the Episcopal Church in the United States authorized trial-use marriage rites for same-sex couples in 2015. On the words of 6:9 themselves, writers argue both ways. Robert Gagnon reads the pair as naming same-sex intercourse itself, with malakoi as males who take the female role. Dale Martin argues that arsenokoitai pointed to some kind of economic exploitation by means of sex, not necessarily homosexual sex, and that malakos is better rendered "effeminate"; he adds that he does not claim to know what arsenokoites meant, only that no one does. The notes on 6:9 set out the evidence.

Divided. The United Methodist Book of Discipline long called homosexual practice "incompatible with Christian teaching"; in 2024 the General Conference removed that language. On the words of 6:9 themselves, writers argue both ways. Robert Gagnon reads the pair as naming same-sex intercourse itself, with malakoi as males who take the female role. Dale Martin argues that arsenokoitai pointed to some kind of economic exploitation by means of sex, not necessarily homosexual sex, and that malakos is better rendered "effeminate"; he adds that he does not claim to know what arsenokoites meant, only that no one does. The notes on 6:9 set out the evidence.

title: Marriage, Singleness and the Short Time
sum: Paul now answers the church's letter (7:1). The Corinthians wrote about sex and marriage, and the chapter is the longest early Christian treatment of the subject. He agrees that singleness is good but says that married people owe each other their bodies in equal measure, and that each has a gift from God. To the married he gives a command of the Lord: no divorce; if the couple separates, no new marriage. To believers married to unbelievers he gives his own ruling: stay, unless the unbeliever leaves.

At the center he states a rule for all the churches: stay in the situation you were in when God called you, whether circumcised or not, slave or free. Then he turns to the "virgins," gives a judgment, not a command, and explains it: the time has been cut short, and the form of this world is passing away. He closes with the case of the widow, who is free to marry "only in the Lord," and says he thinks he has the Spirit of God too.
readings: Read as advice for a particular crisis

Paul's "pressure of the present time" (7:26) and "the time has been cut short" (7:29) may point to a food shortage or to the expected end. On this reading his preference for singleness is for that time, not for always.
Read as a charter for marriage and singleness together
The chapter's pairs, husband and wife, circumcised and uncircumcised, slave and free, put two ways of life on equal footing. Each is a gift (7:7), and neither is a higher rank.
Read as a guide to authority

Paul separates what the Lord commands (7:10), what he himself says (7:12), and what is his judgment (7:25, 40), and still claims the Spirit's guidance. The churches differ on how binding each level is (see the cards).

views.H: The Corinthian letter that Paul answers was probably written by men and women who held that sexual restraint was spiritual (7:1) and perhaps others who held that the body did not matter (6:12-20). In Roman law either spouse could end a marriage by notice, and divorce was common among the elite. Slavery was part of the economy: slaves were freed by owners or bought their own freedom, and freed slaves stayed bound to former owners. A grain shortage under Claudius may be the "pressure" of 7:26.
views.C: Variants affect the KJV ("fasting and" in 7:5, "due benevolence" in 7:3, "by the law" in 7:39, "husband" in 7:14) and the sense of 7:15 ("called us" or "called you"). Scholars debate whether 7:1 is a slogan, whether 7:14 reflects a baptismal custom, and who "his virgin" is (7:36-38). Nearly all scholars hold that the whole chapter is Paul's.
views.L: The chapter is built in pairs: man and woman (7:2-5), unmarried and widowed (7:8-9), married to believers and to unbelievers (7:10-16). The words "remain" and "stay" (7:8, 11, 20, 24, 26, 40) run through the chapter, and the rule about the calling (7:17-24) sits at its center. Paul uses the same "as if not" figure five times in 7:29-31.
views.J: Paul quotes no verse in this chapter but rests on Jewish thinking about marriage (Genesis 2:24; Exodus 21:10), divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1; Hillel and Shammai), mixed marriage (Ezra 10), and circumcision (Genesis 17). 7:19 is a key text for the "Paul within Judaism" reading: circumcision is nothing, but keeping God's commands matters. He expects Jews to stay Jews and Gentiles to stay Gentiles (7:18).
views.T: 7:1-9 and 7:25-38 are the base of the Catholic and Orthodox honor for celibacy and virginity; Luther and Calvin cite the same verses for marriage as the normal calling. 7:10-16 is where the churches' divorce rules begin: the Catholic indissolubility and Pauline privilege, the Protestant grounds of adultery and desertion, the Orthodox economy. 7:14 enters the infant-baptism debates.

deep.b:
Jewish law, Roman law and Jesus' teaching all lie behind 7:10-16. In Deuteronomy 24:1 the husband gives the wife a certificate. In the first century the schools disagreed on grounds: Shammai allowed only serious indecency, Hillel almost anything (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). Roman law had no certificate and no court: either spouse could end the marriage by notice. Jesus' teaching, as the Gospels record it, forbids divorce followed by remarriage, with Matthew adding "except for sexual sin" (Matthew 19:9; compare Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18).

Paul is the earliest writer to apply that teaching. He begins with the Lord's command (7:10-11), which he restates for a Roman setting by including wives. He then goes beyond it for a case Jesus did not address, marriage between a believer and an unbeliever (7:12-16). The result is a short list of rules, and the churches have drawn very different laws from it. David Instone-Brewer has argued that Exodus 21:10-11, which gives a wife food, clothing and marital rights, was understood in Paul's day as grounds for divorce for neglect, and that Paul's talk of the marriage "debt" (7:3-5) and of the deserted believer (7:15) assumes it. Other scholars dispute this.

deep.h: Staying put: circumcision, slavery and the rule of 7:17-24
deep.b:
The center of the chapter is a rule: "each person should live the life the Lord has given him." Paul applies it to circumcision (7:18-19) and slavery (7:21-23), the two great marks of status in his world, and he sets Christ's call above both. A Jew need not try to hide his circumcision, and a Gentile should not be circumcised. A slave need not be anxious about slavery, though a chance at freedom may be taken. In both, Paul claims that a person's standing before God does not depend on the mark.

This rule has had two different lives. In Galatians and Acts, Paul fights to keep Gentiles from being circumcised, and in Acts 16:3 he has Timothy circumcised for the sake of Jews. On slavery, the passage has been read both as a rule that kept slavery in place and as a seed of the idea that no Christian should hold another in bondage. Paul's word to Philemon (verse 16) and the church's long history show that the text did not settle the question by itself.

The question is who "his virgin" is. The father reading gives a straightforward picture: a father decides whether to give his daughter in marriage. The fiancé reading has a man who is engaged and wonders if he is wrong to wait. The spiritual-marriage reading has a couple who live together as celibates, which the church later condemned in the third century. The guardian reading sees a man responsible for a young woman in his household. Each has support in the Greek, and none of them is certain.

All agree on the result: marrying is not a sin, not marrying is better in the present pressure, and no one is bound by a rule. The Plain keeps the words "his virgin" in 7:36-37 and renders the verb of 7:38 with a wide phrase, "sees to the marriage of," so that the reader sees the question. A second crux is the word hyperakmos in 7:36: it can mean "past the bloom of youth," said of the woman (the Plain's choice, which leans toward the father reading), or "strong in passion," said of the man, which many translations follow. The note on 7:36 gives the evidence.

echoes: Genesis 2:24; Exodus 21:10; Deuteronomy 24:1; Ezra 10:3; Malachi 2:16; Mark 10:2; Luke 16:18; Matthew 5:32; Matthew 19:9; Matthew 19:12; Galatians 3:28; Galatians 5:6; Philemon 16; 1 Timothy 5:14; Romans 7:2

settings.what: Paul's answer to the Corinthians' letter about sex in marriage
settings.to: The married and unmarried of the church at Corinth, in reply to what they wrote
settings.when: After the church's letter reached him in Ephesus, probably through Stephanas and his companions (16:17)
settings.why: To correct a view that the spiritual should stay away from sex, by teaching equal, mutual rights and a short break only by agreement. Marriage is not a concession to weakness but a gift, as singleness is.
settings.readers: Believers in a city with many marriages broken or avoided, some drawn to an ascetic ideal, others to sexual freedom (6:12-20).
views: Some Corinthian believers urged sexual abstinence, including within marriage (7:1, 5).
Paul quotes the slogan, qualifies it and lets both marriage and singleness stand as gifts.

settings.what: Advice for the unmarried and widows
settings.to: The unmarried and widowed of the church
settings.when: As part of the same reply
settings.why: To say that staying single is good, as he is, but that those who cannot control desire should marry.
settings.readers: Widows and unmarried believers, some of them young, with no social role outside marriage.

settings.to: Believing couples, both of whom belong to the church
settings.when: Perhaps as he deals with some who wished to leave marriage for the sake of the spirit (a reconstruction; the text does not say)
settings.why: To pass on Jesus' teaching that marriage is not to be ended, and to say what is allowed if a couple does separate. Roman law let either spouse leave, so the rule restrains both husband and wife.
settings.readers: Believers in a Roman colony where divorce was easy and the culture of honor set a high value on leaving a marriage that no longer served the family.
views: The Torah's certificate (Deuteronomy 24:1) and the debate between Hillel and Shammai (Mishnah Gittin 9:10) were the background for Jesus' saying.
Either spouse could end a marriage by notice. Paul's rule is addressed to that practice.

settings.what: Paul's own ruling on marriages between a believer and an unbeliever
settings.by: Paul, without a saying of the Lord
settings.to: Believers married to unbelievers, a new situation in the church
settings.when: After conversion of one spouse in a marriage, which Jesus did not address
settings.why: To keep couples together where the unbeliever agrees to stay, and to release the believer who is deserted. On one reading of 7:14 the believer makes the household holy (the note gives the other readings). The aim is peace and a hope of bringing the spouse to faith.
settings.readers: A church in which many were the first believer in their household, often a wife whose husband worshiped the city's gods.

settings.what: The rule: stay in the calling in which you were called
settings.by: Paul, as his rule 'in all the churches'
settings.to: All the Corinthians, with the examples of circumcised and uncircumcised, slave and free
settings.when: As the center of the chapter, illustrating the answers on marriage
settings.why: To tell believers that conversion does not require a change of social or ethnic status: God's call reaches each person where he or she is, and the status marks count for nothing before God. For circumcision: the Torah binds Jewish men, and Paul does not ask Jews to give it up or Gentiles to take it on. For slavery: the law of Rome made a slave the property of the owner, and Paul does not here address the law.
settings.readers: A church with Jews and Gentiles, slaves, freed slaves and free citizens, who might have thought that a spiritual life required a change of status.
views: Paul gives a general rule of calling, with exceptions.
A principle for the short time
The rule is tied to the 'present pressure' (7:26) and the shortened time (7:29), and is not a permanent social law.

settings.by: Paul, with no word of the Lord
settings.to: Unmarried young women, their fathers, guardians or fiancés (the text is not clear which), and the church
settings.when: As a reply to the church's question 'about the virgins' (7:25)
settings.why: To advise, not command, that remaining unmarried is good in the present pressure, since marriage brings troubles and divided attention. He says plainly that those who marry do not sin.
settings.readers: Families of young women in a church that wondered whether marrying was a lesser path. Paul gives a gentle judgment so no one feels bound.
views: The man in 7:36-38 is a father or guardian.
The man is engaged to the woman.
A couple living together as celibates.
The man is responsible for a young woman in his household.

settings.to: Widows of the church, who may marry whom they wish 'only in the Lord'
settings.when: As the close of the chapter
settings.why: To release widows from the bond of marriage, to allow a new marriage within the faith, and to say that he thinks it is better if she stays single.
settings.readers: Widows who might wonder whether a second marriage was permitted for Christians.

traditions.q: Is the single life a higher calling than marriage?
views: Yes. The Council of Trent (session 24, canon 10) condemns anyone who says it is not "better and more blessed" to remain in virginity or celibacy than to marry. Ordained ministers of the Latin Church, except permanent deacons, are normally chosen from men who live a celibate life (Catechism 1579). The Catechism calls virginity for the sake of the kingdom a sign of the supremacy of the bond with Christ and says marriage and virginity both come from the Lord (1619-1620).
Bishops are usually drawn from monks and must be celibate, while married men may be ordained priests if they marry before ordination.
The Augsburg Confession (article 23) says priests may lawfully marry.

Calvin's commentary on 7:7-9 calls virginity "an excellent gift" given to only a few, and says those who vowed lifelong celibacy without regard to their own capacity acted rashly. The Westminster Confession (24.3) says it is lawful for all sorts of people to marry who can give their consent with judgment.

Article 32 of the Thirty-Nine Articles says Bishops, Priests and Deacons "are not commanded by God's Law, either to vow the estate of single life, or to abstain from marriage," and may marry at their own discretion.

traditions.q: Does 7:10-16 allow divorce and remarriage, and on what grounds?
views: A valid marriage creates a bond that is "perpetual and exclusive" (Catechism 1638), and "a ratified and consummated marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power or for any reason other than death" (Catechism 2382). Separation is allowed (7:11) when living together becomes practically impossible, but the spouses are not free to contract a new union (Catechism 1649). The "Pauline privilege" of 7:15 is set out in canon 1143: a marriage between two unbaptized people is dissolved in favor of the faith when one is baptized, the other departs, and the baptized one marries again.

The Orthodox Church in America says marriage is a lifelong commitment and the Church stands opposed to divorce, yet it permits a second and even a third marriage "by economy," an exception to the rule, with an order of service that bears a penitential character.
Luther allowed divorce for adultery and also treated desertion as a ground for divorce.
The Westminster Confession allows divorce for adultery after marriage (24.5) and for such willful desertion as can no way be remedied by the church or the civil magistrate (24.6).

In July 2002 the General Synod of the Church of England voted that there are circumstances in which a divorced person may be married in church during the lifetime of a former spouse; the decision is left to the individual priest.
The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (article XVIII) describes marriage as "the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime." The article does not address divorce.

traditions.q: Does 7:14 show that the children of believers belong to the covenant, so they should be baptized?
views: Yes. Calvin's commentary on 7:14 says the children of believers are "set apart from others by a sort of exclusive privilege, so as to be reckoned holy in the Church." The Westminster Confession (28.4) says infants of one or both believing parents are to be baptized.
Infants are baptized because baptism rests on God's command, not on the child's faith (Large Catechism, on Baptism, paragraphs 47-60).
Infants are baptized because they are born tainted by original sin (Catechism 1250).
Infants are baptized, chrismated and given Holy Communion at once: "This is the case with infants as well as adults" (Orthodox Church in America).

No. The verse says nothing of baptism, and the unbelieving spouse is also called holy. The 1689 Confession (chapter 29, paragraph 2) says those who "actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ, are the only proper subjects of this ordinance."
Schleitheim (article 1) gives baptism to those who have learned repentance and amendment of life and believe, and excludes infant baptism.

title: Knowledge That Builds Up
sum: The next question from Corinth is about food that has been sacrificed to idols. Some Corinthians said, "We all have knowledge": an idol is nothing and there is one God, so the meat is just meat. Paul agrees with the creed (there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ) but not with how it is used. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up, and "not everyone has this knowledge."

He pictures a believer with knowledge sitting at a banquet in a pagan temple, and a weaker believer who sees him and is "built up" to eat, against his conscience, and so is damaged. The weak person is a brother for whom Christ died. To sin against such a person is to sin against Christ. So Paul will give up meat altogether if that is what love requires. Chapter 9 will show him doing that, and chapter 10 will return to the rules.
readings: Read as a case of weak and strong
The chapter sets the strong (who know that idols are nothing) against the weak (who still feel the pull of the idol). Paul sides with the strong on the creed and with the weak on the practice.
Read as a lesson on love and knowledge
Knowledge is good but unfinished (8:2); love is how a person is known by God (8:3). The chapter makes love the test of knowledge.
Read as the first panel of a three-part argument
Chapters 8-10 form one unit: principle (8), example (9), warning and rules (10). Eating in a temple is treated here as harm to others, and in 10:14-22 as a danger to the one who eats.

views.H: Temples in Corinth held public meals; meat from sacrifices was sold in the market; clubs and families held dinners in temple dining rooms. A Christian invited to a wedding or a patron's dinner could not easily refuse. Archaeology has found dining rooms at the Asklepieion and at the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore. Jews avoided such food, and the Jerusalem decree (Acts 15:29) told Gentile believers to do the same, though Paul does not cite it.
views.C: Variants include "habit" or "conscience" in 8:7, the order of the clauses in 8:8, and "is destroyed" or "will perish" in 8:11. Scholars debate how the unit 8:1-11:1 relates to the Jerusalem decree and whether chapter 10's stricter line comes from a different letter, though most take 8-10 as one argument. The slogans of 8:1 and 8:4 are probably quoted.
views.L: The chapter is in three movements: knowledge and love (8:1-3), the creed (8:4-6) and the weak (8:7-13). Within it the verbs "build up" (8:1, 10) and "destroy" (8:11) frame the two outcomes. Paul uses a sorites-like escalation: eat, the weak eat, the weak perish, I sin against Christ. The creed of 8:6 is in a balanced two-part form that is often thought to be an early hymn or confession.
views.J: 8:4-6 is built on the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), and the pairing "God" and "Lord" reworks it around Jesus. Jewish teachers also debated whether the idol or the demon behind it had power (Deuteronomy 32:17; Psalm 96:5), and the tradition of avoiding idol food runs from Exodus 34:15 through Daniel and Tobit to the Mishnah's tractate Avodah Zarah. Jewish readers disagree on whether 8:6 stays within Jewish monotheism.
views.T: 8:6 fills the Christological debates. 8:13 and Romans 14 give the Catholic teaching on scandal (Catechism 2284-2287) and the Protestant teaching on Christian liberty. 8:11 is a proof text in the debate on whether a believer can be lost.

deep.b:
Chapters 8 to 10 read as one argument. In chapter 8 Paul gives the principle: knowledge must be ruled by love. In chapter 9 he gives himself as the example, giving up his rights as an apostle for the sake of the gospel. In chapter 10 he warns from Israel's history and gives the rules: flee idolatry, eat what is sold in the market without asking, and do not eat if someone says it was sacrificed. Margaret Mitchell's study (Paul and the Rhetoric of Reconciliation) reads the whole letter as one argument urging unity, and chapters 8 to 10 as part of it.

Chapter 8 does not settle everything. It says that eating in a temple harms the weak, but not yet that it is wrong in itself; 10:14-22 says that too. Reading chapter 8 alone could suggest that Paul allows temple meals, and reading chapter 10 alone could suggest that he forbids all idol food. The two together show both limits.

deep.h: Idol food in the early church
deep.b:
The question did not go away. Acts 15:29 puts "food sacrificed to idols" in the Jerusalem decree for Gentile believers, and Revelation 2:14 and 2:20 charge the churches in Pergamum and Thyatira with it. The Didache (6:3), an early Christian manual, says to bear what you are able about food but to be exceedingly careful about food sacrificed to idols, which it calls the service of dead gods. In Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho (35), Trypho says he has heard that many who confess Jesus eat meats offered to idols, and Justin calls the teachers of such people heretics.

Paul's position in chapters 8-10 is more careful than any of these. He holds that the idol is nothing, that food does not bring us closer to God, and yet that the Christian must flee idol worship and not hurt others. His approach was neither the stricter rule of Revelation nor a free pass.

Paul calls them "the weak" and says their conscience is weak because they are still used to idols (8:7). Most take them to be Gentile believers for whom eating idol meat still felt like worship. Others think of Jewish believers who kept the food laws, as in Romans 14, though Paul's talk of idols points to Gentiles. Paul does not call them wrong. He asks the strong to give way, not the weak to catch up, though he hopes they will grow. The strong are likely to be better-off members who could afford temple banquets and had social ties that made refusing awkward.

echoes: Deuteronomy 6:4; Isaiah 45:5; Psalm 96:5; Deuteronomy 32:17; Exodus 34:15; Acts 15:29; Revelation 2:14; Romans 14:1; Romans 14:13; Romans 14:21; John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Galatians 4:9

settings.what: Paul's answer on food sacrificed to idols
settings.to: The church at Corinth, both those who ate idol food and those who could not
settings.when: As the second of his answers to the church's letter ("Now about," as in 7:1, 7:25)
settings.why: To keep knowledge from being used as a weapon: love decides what to do with a right. The weak are brothers and sisters for whom Christ died, and harming them is sin against Christ. He prepares the way for chapters 9 and 10.
settings.readers: A church with better-off members who had friends and patrons that invited them to temple meals, and poorer or newer members who had been idol worshipers and felt it.
views: The weak are Gentile converts for whom the meat still meant the idol.
The weak are Jewish believers who kept the food laws, as in Romans 14.

traditions.q: May a Christian eat food that has been offered to idols, and how far must love limit the freedom?
views: Scandal is "an attitude or behavior which leads another to do evil" (Catechism 2284), and anyone who uses power in a way that leads others to do wrong becomes guilty of it (Catechism 2287). Aquinas separates the scandal of the weak ("little ones"), for which some goods may be deferred, concealed or given up, from the scandal of the Pharisees, which is not to be yielded to (Summa II-II, question 43, articles 7-8).

The Orthodox Church receives the Jerusalem decree of Acts 15:29, which names food sacrificed to idols, as part of Scripture. The early Christian Didache (6:3) says: "concerning food, bear what you are able; but against that which is sacrificed to idols be exceedingly careful; for it is the service of dead gods."

In matters of indifference believers may give way to the weak in faith with a good conscience, but in a time of confession they must not yield to adversaries who press such things (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, article 10).
Calvin's Institutes (3.19, on Christian liberty) takes up offense given and taken, and the Westminster Confession (20.2) says God alone is Lord of the conscience.

The passage has been used in Baptist arguments over other practices. Daniel Akin, a Southern Baptist leader, wrote in 2006 that abstaining from alcohol "is consistent with the ethic of love for believers and unbelievers alike (1 Cor. 8:13; 9:19-22; 10:32-33)."

Schleitheim (article 4) calls for separation from "the evil and from the wickedness which the devil planted in the world," naming "abominations" such as drinking houses and civic affairs, and says believers shall not have fellowship with them.

traditions.q: Does 8:6 place Jesus within the one God of the Shema?
views: Yes. The Catholic Church confesses the Son as God with the Father in the Nicene Creed.

Chrysostom (Homily 20 on 1 Corinthians) says Paul does not hand out the names as if each belonged to one person alone: "the Scripture uses also often to interchange them." On his reading, calling the Father "God" does not cast the Son out "from being God."
Yes. The Westminster Confession (chapter 2, section 3) confesses "three persons, of one substance, power, and eternity."
No. The Racovian Catechism identifies the one God as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and teaches that Jesus is the human Son of God, not the one God.

No. Jehovah is the Father, the "one God" of 8:6; the New World Translation's study note on 8:6 ties "one God" to Deuteronomy 6:4 and Isaiah 43-45. Jesus is the "one Lord" through whom all things came.

Yes, in a different sense. The United Pentecostal Church statement of faith says there is one God, who has revealed himself as Father, through his Son in redemption, and as the Holy Spirit, and that Jesus Christ is God manifested in the flesh.

traditions.q: Can a brother or sister 'for whom Christ died' be destroyed?
views: The elect persevere to the end (Westminster Confession, chapter 17; Canons of Dort, fifth head). 8:11 warns of what the strong would do to a weak believer's faith, and God keeps his own.
Yes. In Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints (1751), Wesley argued that a saint may "so fall from God as to perish everlastingly."
Grace can be lost by mortal sin (Catechism 1861); 8:11 shows the gravity of scandal, which can lead a brother to ruin.
The Augsburg Confession (article 12) says that for those who have fallen after baptism there is remission of sins whenever they are converted.
True believers endure to the end (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 5), so 8:11 is read as a warning of the damage that appears to destroy, or of a person who only seemed to be a believer.

Chrysostom (Homily 20 on 1 Corinthians) treats the danger as real. He asks the strong, "do you permit him to perish, after the salvation so wrought," and lists among the charges against them that the man is a brother and that Christ died for him.
